clinicalPearls: Caused by biallelic variants in ACO2, encoding mitochondrial aconitase (aconitate hydratase 2), the tricarboxylic-acid-cycle iron-sulphur enzyme that isomerises citrate to isocitrate through the intermediate cis-aconitate.

The classic severe phenotype is infantile cerebellar-retinal degeneration, with truncal hypotonia, developmental arrest or regression, seizures, progressive microcephaly and retinal or optic degeneration.
A milder end of the allelic spectrum is recessive isolated optic atrophy, presenting to ophthalmology without the full encephalopathy.
Neuroimaging characteristically shows progressive cerebellar and cerebral atrophy.
The combination of retinal degeneration or optic atrophy with cerebellar signs should prompt consideration of ACO2.
The labile iron-sulphur cluster makes the enzyme vulnerable to oxidative stress, linking the disorder mechanistically to iron-sulphur cluster biology.
Diagnosis rests on ACO2 sequencing supported by reduced aconitase enzyme activity; no curative therapy exists.
reference.pathophysiology: ACO2 encodes mitochondrial aconitase, a citric-acid-cycle enzyme containing a labile [4Fe-4S] iron-sulphur cluster that catalyses the reversible isomerisation of citrate to isocitrate via the intermediate cis-aconitate. Pathogenic biallelic variants reduce enzyme activity and destabilise the iron-sulphur cluster, impairing oxidative energy metabolism and increasing susceptibility to oxidative damage in the highly energy-dependent neurons of the cerebellum and the photoreceptors of the retina. This produces a clinical spectrum ranging from severe infantile cerebellar-retinal degeneration to isolated recessive optic atrophy. Inheritance is autosomal recessive, and the disorder is distinct from cytosolic aconitase (ACO1/IRP1), which principally regulates cellular iron homeostasis.
additionalDifferentials: Other genetic causes of infantile cerebellar-retinal degeneration
Isolated or syndromic optic atrophies (OPA1, WFS1/Wolfram, OPA3/Costeff)
Leigh syndrome and other mitochondrial encephalopathies
Congenital disorders of glycosylation with cerebellar atrophy
Iron-sulphur cluster assembly disorders, including ISCU myopathy (the historical combined 'muscle aconitase' deficiency)
Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses (retinal degeneration with neuroregression)
additionalInvestigations: ACO2 gene sequencing or a mitochondrial gene panel
Aconitase enzyme activity assay in fibroblasts or muscle
Brain MRI to assess cerebellar and cerebral atrophy
Ophthalmological assessment with electroretinography and optical coherence tomography
Blood and CSF lactate with a general metabolic screen
Respiratory-chain and related tricarboxylic-acid-cycle studies where available
redFlags: Developmental regression with progressive microcephaly in infancy
Rapidly evolving cerebellar atrophy on serial imaging
Combined retinal degeneration and optic atrophy alongside neurological signs
reference.prognosis: The severe infantile cerebellar-retinal form is progressive, with profound disability and early mortality, whereas isolated optic atrophy at the milder end follows a more limited, chiefly visual course.
pitfalls: Confusing ACO2 (mitochondrial) disease with the historical combined 'muscle aconitase' deficiency, which reflects iron-sulphur cluster assembly (ISCU) myopathy.
Overlooking ACO2 when the presentation appears to be isolated optic atrophy.
Attributing progressive microcephaly and cerebellar atrophy to a static perinatal insult.
Assuming that a normal early eye examination excludes later retinal degeneration.
references: Inherited optic neuropathy and retinal degeneration guidelines
management: No disease-specific cure exists, so management is supportive and symptom-directed for this mitochondrial disorder
Antiepileptic therapy to control seizures in the infantile cerebellar-retinal form
Multidisciplinary neurodevelopmental support with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy for hypotonia and developmental impairment
Feeding assessment and nutritional support, with tube feeding where bulbar or feeding difficulty occurs
Low-vision support and ophthalmological follow-up for the retinal degeneration or optic atrophy
Consider an empirical mitochondrial antioxidant and cofactor regimen while avoiding known oxidative stressors
Genetic counselling for the autosomal recessive inheritance, with palliative and family support in the severe progressive phenotype
